name: Happy's change journal: a weekly review of what it did and remembered, 'undo that' for its last write, and forgetting a conversation on request
description: Happy records every write its tools make for a parent in one journal, so each parent can ask, or read in one Sunday text, what Happy did for them and what it kept in memory that week (the notes it saved and the chat snapshots the memory hook filed), and can say 'undo that' to reverse Happy's own last write to a list, a reminder, the calendar or the household facts from the past 24 hours, after seeing what will be reversed. Anything already sent (a text, an email, a print job) cannot be recalled, a saved note is corrected by asking Happy to change it, and clearing what one conversation left in memory stays Tony's job at the Mac, previewed first.
example: Sunday text: 'This week I set 4 reminders for you, added 6 items to Groceries, sent 2 texts to Jordan, asked you for 1 approval (given) and saved 3 notes to memory.' Or Tony texts 'undo that' after Happy replaced the furnace filter size in the household facts with the wrong one; Happy shows the old value, waits for a yes and restores it.
how:
Journal (shared): each in-house write tool (household store, Reminders bridge, calendar write, the reminder-pinning hook) writes a row from inside the tool, where the old value is known: who asked, when, which tool, the inverse call. `openclaw audit --kind tool_action` gives names and outcomes only. Memory saves (F041) are made with the built-in `write` and `edit` tools, not an in-house tool, so their rows come from an observe-only `after_tool_call` hook on those two tools, filtered to the memory files: who, when, which file and the text saved, with no inverse. The bundled session-memory hook that F041 also turns on is a second writer: at each reset and each daily or idle rollover it saves the recent messages of a chat to a dated file in the same memory folder. A hook writes that file, not a tool, so it leaves no `after_tool_call` row, and the review counts those files from their dated names. Approval rows come from the asking hook's `onResolution` callback. Review (G006, F085): a command automation renders the Sunday text with no model; a read tool returns only the asker's rows. Undo (CRT-01): an `undo_last` tool on `

-main`, limited by a `before_tool_call` hook to the requester's rows from the last 24 hours, shows the row, waits for a yes, runs the inverse; for a row with no inverse (a memory save) it says so, and the parent asks Happy to correct or delete the note. Forgetting (F085): `openclaw memory forget --agent --session --dry-run`, then without it, then hand-delete the `curatedWrites` lines.
caveats: The journal rows for lists, reminders, the calendar and household facts must be written by the write tools themselves from the start, with the old value: rows written by an after_tool_call hook carry no old value and would have to be redone for undo. Memory saves are the one exception: they go through the built-in write and edit tools, are logged by a hook with no inverse, and so appear in the review but cannot be undone.
Sent things cannot be recalled (a text to the other parent, an email to the owner, a print job, a Sonos announcement), so the reply has to say so at the time of sending.

Undo covers only Happy's own writes: if a parent has since edited the same reminder or event on a phone the inverse could overwrite that edit, so the tool should refuse when the item changed after Happy wrote it.

The Reminders bridge (F030) was specified with no delete, so undo adds one, and it must accept only item ids the journal recorded as created by Happy, enforced inside the tool and not left to the model.

Most 'undo' requests are corrections that the same write tool already handles with a second write; undo earns its place for overwritten household facts, where the old value would otherwise be gone, so it is the second step and can be left out without changing the journal or the review.
OpenClaw's own ledger leaves out arguments on purpose, so the in-house table that holds item text and recipients needs a retention limit, which is not yet defined.

Forgetting works per conversation, not per topic: the forget command selects whole sessions, deletes at once unless `--dry-run` is passed, leaves the transcripts, and only lists the notes Happy wrote itself, which Tony then deletes by hand.

The review of actions, the memory list and the week-ahead brief (F014) would otherwise be three Sunday texts to the same parent, so the first two go out as one; lines in MEMORY.md carry no date, so the memory list is reliable only when it comes from the per-write record.

The journal row for a memory save keeps a copy of the saved text in the household store. The forget command does not clean other plugins' stores or backups, so correcting or deleting a note, and forgetting a conversation, must also delete the matching journal rows, or the forgotten text lives on there.

Not everything Happy keeps in memory passes through a tool. Once per-person memory (F041) turns on the session-memory hook, the recent messages of each chat are saved to a dated file at every reset or daily rollover, and OpenClaw's memory provenance page says its admission rules are not applied to session hooks. The weekly text has to count those files as well, or it under-reports what was kept.

A sick-day dose row (CRT-10) is a household-store write, so the journal would still hold a child's health note after the row's own 14-day deletion. The journal's retention rule has to drop those rows at the same time, or record them without their text.
corrections: 'Forget what I said about X works' (9 Oct description) is not a platform ability: memory forget selects whole sessions by id, hook source or participant, never by topic or message text, and reworded copies are outside its cleanup. Topic-level forgetting is a hand edit of the memory file.

'Promote via openclaw memory promote --apply' will usually promote nothing a parent just confirmed: by default a candidate needs a 0.75 score, three recalls and three distinct queries. Either pass lower thresholds or write the confirmed line to MEMORY.md directly.
unverified: Whether turning on message audit rows needs a Gateway restart: the audit CLI page says restart, the Gateway audit page says audit settings apply without one.
Retention for the custom side-effect table in home-store is undefined.
With dreaming switched off (roadmap decision) the session-exclusion setting has little to act on today; its effect was not tested.
The memory-wiki dashboards named on 9 Oct (privacy review, stale pages) are documented, but the plugin is not enabled on this install.
What a forget preview reports on this install was not run; the docs say direct edits are listed for review and are not given per-entry lineage.

That an `after_tool_call` hook on the built-in `write` and `edit` tools is handed the file path and the text written, so that each memory save becomes one dated journal row; this was read in the hook types, not run. Without those rows the weekly list cannot tell this week's saves from older lines in MEMORY.md, which carry no date.
That an approval hook's `onResolution` callback is a workable source for the 'approvals given' line; it was read in the hook reference, not run, and no approval hook exists in the config repo yet.
That no built-in undo for tool effects exists anywhere in 2026.9.7: searches of the installed docs for undo, rewind, revert and checkpoint found none, but the dist source was not read.
Whether the Reminders command-line tool and the calendar server return stable item ids that an inverse can target; neither is installed yet.
Whether `memory forget` for a conversation also removes the dated file the session-memory hook saved for it; the deletion page opened in this run does not name those files.
safety: The review only reports, and each parent sees only their own rows, enforced in the read tool's code. Undo is the write half: it reverses a write the same person's agent made, adds no recipient or data source, and its hook blocks on error. Forgetting deletes memory at once, so it stays an operator command at the Mac.

name: Recovery card for the second adult (a bus factor of one)
description: One printed page and a sealed envelope so Jordan can tell that Happy is down and bring it back after a power cut while Tony is travelling, and, once the stop phrase exists (G005), pause it. Today every recovery step, including the disk unlock after a reboot, depends on Tony being at home.
example: Trigger: a power cut while Tony is abroad. Happy stops answering and Jordan opens the card.
how: No new software. The card lists: (1) how to tell: no reply within a few minutes; also add Jordan as a second recipient of the existing dead-man alert. (2) The pause phrase, added to the card once G005 is built: sending it harms nothing, but G005 makes lifting a stop a command-line step at the Mac, so the card either carries that step for Jordan or says plainly that a pause lasts until Tony is back. (3) After a power cut the Mac waits at the FileVault screen: type the password from the envelope at the Mac, then log in the happy user so Messages runs. The gateway and its helpers are launch agents in the happy user's login session (M0 sign-off), so they start by themselves once happy is logged in and not before. Apple's remote unlock over SSH needs Apple silicon, macOS 26 or later, Remote Login on and a network connection, and the roadmap notes it works from the home network only, so it does not help someone who is away. (4) The commands that may be needed if Happy is still silent: logged in as happy, 'openclaw gateway status' and 'openclaw gateway restart' (the docs say not to chain stop and start). The house scripts are the operator's repair tools and go with the second envelope: from Tony's admin account 'happy-inspect ready' is a read-only check, while 'happy-deploy --restart' also restarts (ready within about ten seconds at M0) but first applies whatever config is staged, so it is not the card's restart step. (5) Who to call. The envelope holds what the card needs and where the config repo and backups are. Separately, set a Legacy Contact on the Apple Accounts involved so the account behind Happy's iMessage identity can be recovered in the worst case; Apple's legacy access leaves out Keychain passwords, so the API keys still depend on the nightly backup (its checklist lines are now in G008). Rehearse once: Tony leaves the house, Jordan restarts the Mac and brings Happy back from the card. Least privilege, from review: the happy user holds a secure token on this Mac (read with sysadminctl in this review), and Apple's FileVault management page says unlocking needs a secure token and, on Apple silicon, volume ownership. If happy's password unlocks the disk at the startup screen, that one step also logs happy in, which is all a power cut needs. The first envelope then holds only happy's password and the admin credential goes in a second envelope for repairs. Confirm this at the rehearsal before relying on it.
depends_on: decision: what goes in Jordan's envelope: the happy user's password only (enough for a restart if it unlocks the disk; it already opens every person's agent data) or also an admin credential (break-glass access that adds Tony's own account and the config repo)
G005 stop phrase, only for the pause step: the rest of the card can be printed and rehearsed before it exists
decision: whether Jordan's card carries the step that lifts a stop (G005 makes lifting command-line only, at the Mac) or a pause simply lasts until Tony is back
the existing nightly backup (its checklist lines are now in G008)
a small UPS (already suggested in the roadmap)
caveats: The envelope is a credential on paper. The happy password alone already opens every person's agent data, because the gateway keeps it under that account; an admin credential adds Tony's own account and the config repo. That is the price of not being locked out.
A UPS only bridges short cuts. A long outage still ends at the FileVault screen.
Legacy Contact access needs the access key and a death certificate. It is for the worst case, not for a business trip.
If Apple locks the Apple Account that Happy uses, nobody at home can fix it quickly, and iMessage is the only channel.

The pause is one-way for Jordan unless the card says how to lift it: the stop entry (G005) keeps a stop in a file and makes lifting it a command-line step at the Mac, so the card's restart step is not expected to lift it. Until G005 is built the card has no pause step at all.
safety: Nothing is granted to any agent and no secret is typed into chat or stored in Happy's memory. The control plane stays Tony's in normal operation; the envelope is a deliberate exception that is obvious once used, because it is sealed.
unverified: Whether a standard, non-admin macOS account for Jordan can be enabled to unlock FileVault at boot on this Mac; the Apple page read in this run does not say who may unlock.
Whether the happy user is a volume owner and is offered at the FileVault startup screen. The secure token status was read; the unlock itself was not tried.

name: Paired-device command deny list before any Mac or phone is paired (computer.act, Mac host commands, iPhone data commands), plus the off switches
description: Make 'no agent can drive, run commands on or view any Mac, or pull personal data (location, contacts, calendar, reminders, photos, motion) from a paired phone' an explicit Gateway setting instead of a side effect of no app being installed, and write down the three ways to switch computer control off. No Mac or phone is paired as a node today (the two Control UI entries on Tony's iPhone are operator consoles, not nodes), so the family sees no change; it is the gate the iPhone app (OCL-01) and the screen-control pilot (MAC-02) must pass first.
example: Tony adds the deny list to the config repo now, before any Mac or phone is paired. Later, during a pilot, 'Happy, stop everything' also halts desk, and he can flip the switch in the Mac app or remove the Accessibility grant.
how: Add `computer.act` to `gateway.nodes.commands.deny` in happy-config, and while no Mac node is wanted also every desktop host command the docs list as arriving with a Mac pairing: `system.run`, `system.run.prepare`, `system.which`, `browser.proxy`, `browser.proxy.upload.v1`, `mcp.tools.call.v1`, `screen.snapshot` and `desktop.stream`. A deny entry always wins over platform defaults and allow entries, matches exact command names, withholds the command (for `computer.act`, together with the node's `computer` capability) and is logged. The list is Gateway-wide, so the same change carries the phone ceiling for the iPhone app entry (OCL-01): deny the iOS default data commands (`location.get`, `contacts.search`, `calendar.events`, `reminders.list`, `photos.latest`, `motion.activity`, `motion.pedometer`) and the four push-to-talk commands (`talk.ptt.start`, `talk.ptt.stop`, `talk.ptt.cancel`, `talk.ptt.once`), which any node that advertises talk otherwise gets by default and which come off the list only when Talk (VOX-01) is set up; keep every opt-in command the docs list (`camera.snap`, `camera.clip`, `camera.ptz.control`, `screen.record`, `health.summary`, `contacts.add`, `calendar.add`, `reminders.add`, `sms.send`, `sms.search`) out of `gateway.nodes.commands.allow`, and set `gateway.nodes.pluginTools.enabled: false` so a paired device cannot publish tools to agents. Keep `computer` absent from every agent's tool lists; the per-person agents already deny `group:nodes`, which contains it, and the inbox agent denies every tool. Pairing is already manual-only in the config repo since M0 (`gateway.nodes.pairing.autoApproveLocal: false` and `sshVerify: false`; SSH-verified pairing is otherwise on by default), so keep both and do not use setup links for a Mac, since a setup link can still approve a node's first command surface automatically. The happy-inspect posture check reads only the first of the two; add `sshVerify`, the deny list and `pluginTools.enabled` to it. Leave `gateway.nodes.pairing.autoApproveCidrs` unset (it is off unless set), so no device is approved by network address alone. The deny list covers paired nodes; control of the Gateway's own desktop is a separate route that the docs say needs the `cua-computer` plugin explicitly enabled on the Gateway host, so never run `openclaw plugins enable cua-computer` on the Mac mini, and add a posture-check line that fails if that plugin shows as explicitly enabled, so the rule is checked and not only remembered. For reference, the documented gate stack for screen control is: tool policy exposes `computer` to an agent; gateway command policy; device pairing and then a second, distinct approval of the node's command surface; the switch inside the Mac app; and the macOS permissions. Exec approvals gate shell commands on a node, not clicks. Off switches during a pilot: (1) put the deny line back (command-policy changes reach connected nodes under the default hybrid reload, with no restart); (2) the G005 kill file checked in the desk hook; (3) on the Mac, turn off 'Allow Computer Control' (rechecked at each invocation) or revoke Accessibility.
caveats: Without this, once OpenClaw.app is installed on any family Mac, its pairing is approved and the macOS permissions are granted, pointer and keyboard control is available to any agent later given `computer` and to any caller with operator write access, because `computer.act` is in the macOS default allowlist and the app switch defaults on.
The deny list is global, not per Mac. The per-Mac controls are the pairing approval and the switch inside the app, so a pilot that lifts a deny entry lifts it for every paired node.
`screen.record` is already off unless explicitly allowed; `screen.snapshot` and `desktop.stream` are not, once a pairing that declares them is approved.

The two-step approval (device, then command surface) is not unconditional: SSH-verified pairing and setup-code enrollment can approve a node's first surface automatically. SSH-verified pairing is already switched off in this config; setup codes remain.
The same pairing that would arm `computer.act` also brings shell execution, a browser proxy, node MCP calls and a desktop stream, which is why the deny list names those commands too.

The deny list does not empty a device's command list. OpenClaw's default table still allows `camera.list`, `device.info`, `device.status` and `system.notify` on an iPhone, those four plus `camera.ptz.status` and `device.apps` (the list of installed apps) on a Mac, and the Canvas panel commands for the Mac app. The same page says the current Mac app does not declare the device and personal-data commands, so read each device's declared commands at pairing and add to the deny list any of these that is not wanted.
safety: Pure tightening. It turns an implicit state into a limit in config that a prompt cannot change.
unverified: That deny entries for system.run and the other host commands apply exactly as for computer.act; the docs state the rule for exact command names in general.

That denying browser.proxy and mcp.tools.call.v1 for nodes leaves the sandboxed research browser and any MCP servers on the Gateway itself untouched. No node is paired today; check right after the change.

Whether `gateway.nodes.commands.deny` also blocks the `computer` tool's Gateway-desktop route (`target: "gateway"`); the docs describe a deny entry as withholding a command from a node's advertised surface.

Which command name sits behind the iPhone app's 'Screen snapshot' capability: the docs list `screen.snapshot` as a desktop host command and do not name the phone's, so read the phone's declared commands at pairing (OCL-01) and deny that one by its exact name.

name: Screen-control pilot: one stateless desk agent on a clean, resettable Mac VM (app setup, watching view and go-live test included)
description: An experimental pilot, parked until there is a chore worth it: a dedicated agent with no memory and no other tools is the only holder of `computer`, and it drives a clean macOS virtual machine with no Apple Account, Messages or saved passwords, never happy's own desktop. A parent's agent hands it one bounded task and gets a short text result back; no family task is approved for it today.
example: Operator pilot, not a family text yet: Tony gives desk one synthetic task from the acceptance set (a sample file on the clean desk, with a result that can be checked as a file). desk answers 'done, saved as result.txt' or 'stopped: a sign-in window appeared'.
how: Clean desk (MAC-03): a macOS guest on the Mac mini built with Apple's Virtualization framework (for example the Lume CLI) and reset to a known snapshot before every run; OpenClaw.app is installed inside the guest, paired as its own node and granted Accessibility and Screen Recording there; files move only through the File Transfer plugin limited to one folder. Desk agent (MAC-02): `agents.entries.desk` with memory off, `tools.profile: minimal`, `computer` added and everything else denied, reached only by `sessions_spawn` from a parent's agent; because every Happy agent runs sandboxed and `computer` is on the sandbox default deny list, it must also be named in desk's sandbox tool allow list (`tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow`), the same second gate the research browser needs; a `before_tool_call` hook allowlists actions, checks the kill file and returns `requireApproval` on the first action of each run. Around it: Screen Sharing inside the VM only, so a person can watch, and a ten-task acceptance test with three planted-instruction cases.
depends_on: MAC-04 deny entries for `computer.act` and `screen.snapshot` lifted for the pilot; the deny list is Gateway-wide and not per device, so no other Mac may be paired while the pilot runs, and if the iPhone app (OCL-01) is paired its approved command list is re-read first
disk and memory on the Mac mini for a macOS guest
a route from the guest to the loopback-bound gateway (tailnet identity or SSH tunnel) and a firewall rule limiting the guest to the gateway address
`gateway.nodes.commands.allow` entries for the file commands
F019 spawn pattern
G005 kill switch
G009 family delivery
existing on-demand eval harness (for the acceptance test)
a named family chore that no app or script already handles (none approved today)
caveats: The guest is not empty of secrets: OpenClaw.app inside it is signed in to the family gateway, so until the app is shown to run as a node with no operator rights, the agent driving the screen can open a console to everything the clean desk was built to keep away.

The gateway is bound to loopback and published only through Tailscale Serve, so the guest needs an SSH tunnel, its own tailnet identity or a wider gateway bind, and each of those changes the M0 baseline and needs its own review.
Pairing the Mac app pairs a whole node: shell execution, a browser proxy, node MCP calls and a desktop stream arrive together with pointer control.
A hook sees typed parameters and not meaning, so an action allowlist cannot stop the model clicking the wrong thing, and what exists on the controlled desktop is the real boundary.
The approval on the first action only proves that a parent started the task: the dozens of clicks after it run unreviewed, and the prompt is text only with no screenshot.
Red-team research on computer-use agents reports injected on-screen instructions succeeding in a large share of attempts, so the tool's built-in warning to the model is a tripwire and not a control.
A desktop that is never reset is the agent's memory, because files, open windows and the clipboard carry over from one run, or one parent, to the next.

Whether Computer Control works inside a macOS guest with a virtual display, and whether an approval raised inside a spawned desk run reaches the asking parent's chat, are both untested, and a pass on the acceptance test shows usefulness, not safety.

In OpenClaw 2026.9.7 the `computer` tool can also target the Gateway's own desktop once the `cua-computer` plugin is enabled on the Gateway host, and with no target given it tries a configured Gateway computer first. Never enable that plugin on the Mac mini, and have the hook require `target: "node"` with the guest's node id on every call, so a run can never land on happy's desktop.
safety: desk reads untrusted content (the screen) and holds no memory, accounts or message tool; its ways out are whatever the controlled desktop can reach. The trifecta counts as respected only after the app's operator access inside the guest is removed or proven absent, guest egress is limited to the gateway, and the guest is reset before each run. Never-list items stay off that desktop.
unverified: That `before_tool_call` receives the `computer` tool's action parameters in `event.params` the same way it does for other built-in tools.
That a spawned desk run returns its result to the requester under the family's session-visibility settings (the roadmap lists the same open question for research).

Where a plugin approval raised inside a spawned desk run is delivered. The docs promise same-chat approval for requests that originate from a chat and block a call that has no approval route; if the sub-run does not count as coming from the parent's iMessage chat, every desk task would fail closed.

Live behaviour of the hook on `computer` calls. The installed source wraps every built-in tool, `computer` included, with the before_tool_call hook, and the tool's schema has `action`, `node`, `text`, `app` and `url` parameters, but this was read, not run.

That OpenClaw.app's Computer Control (its TCC grants, its capture path and its 'verified unlocked desktop' check) works inside a macOS guest VM with a virtual display, including a guest running without a display window.
How to restrict a Lume guest's network to one host address.
Whether the Mac app can run in the guest as a node with no operator scopes.

Apple's licence for the installed macOS 27. The macOS Tahoe 26 licence, read in an earlier run, allows up to two additional macOS instances in virtual machines on an Apple-branded computer for personal, non-commercial use.
The guest's memory cost. OpenClaw's macOS VM page asks for about 60 GB of free disk per VM and does not state memory.

name: OpenClaw iPhone app on Tony's phone: chat with files, tap approvals, then Talk mode (device commands denied first; operator only)
description: Tony can also reach Happy in the free OpenClaw iPhone app, on his phone only: a native chat that takes photos, PDFs and other files, a native approval inbox and, as a second and experimental step, Talk mode, a spoken back-and-forth with his own agent. The Control UI already on his phone takes uploads and resolves approvals, so the app adds only the share sheet, an offline queue, the native inbox and Talk; realtime voice is a later option that swaps the Talk loop for a live call with an OpenAI voice model, with the raw audio going to OpenAI on its own key and budget.
example: Tony attaches a 12-page camp packet PDF in the app with + -> File and asks 'what do I have to sign, and by when?'. With Talk set up, he presses the Action Button and says: 'what is on tomorrow, and do I need to pack anything for soccer?'
how: 1. Ceiling (HOM-08): the wave-A deny list (MAC-04) is deployed, with `gateway.nodes.pluginTools.enabled: false`. 2. Install and pair (OCL-01, IPH-01): the App Store app on Tony's iPhone, with a setup code from the Control UI or `openclaw qr` over the Tailscale Serve URL; one code issues a node session and an operator session, so read the approved command list afterwards. No agent gets the built-in nodes tool; uploads pass the F002 gate or `gateway.uploads.enabled: false`. 3. Talk (VOX-01, experimental): take the four push-to-talk commands off the deny list, set a `talk.provider`, and leave `tts.modelOverrides.allowProvider` off; the loop is Apple Speech recognition, Gateway chat, then `talk.speak`. OpenClaw's Talk page says the native loop sends the transcript through the active session, which in the app is the chat that is open, so Tony's Talk runs on the agent he has picked there (tony-main), with that agent's tools and memory. `talk.agentId` is a separate setting: the one gateway-wide fallback owner for a Talk session that arrives without an agent-prefixed key. Set it explicitly to a memory-less agent, so that such a session never lands on an agent that holds memory. 4. Later (VOX-02): a `talk.realtime` block with `provider` openai, `transport` webrtc and `brain` agent-consult.

Tailscale on the phone (already needed for the Control UI)

decision: Full or Limited operator access on Tony's phone (start Limited with `openclaw qr --limited`: the Control UI already on the phone keeps admin, so nothing is given up; Full is what lets the app itself review approvals in general and open its Talk settings pages)
the local privacy gate in F002 extended to Gateway client uploads, or uploads switched off
a written device-revocation step for a lost phone
for Talk: a Talk speech provider under `talk.provider` (the local speech engine from F003 if it works for Talk, which is untested), or accept the iPhone system-voice fallback
for the realtime option only: an OpenAI Platform key dedicated to voice with its own spend cap, and a decision on Zero Data Retention for the organisation that owns that key
decision (only if a second adult's phone is ever wanted): a verified per-person identity with gateway.roles, proven on a test device first
caveats: The app is a chat client, an operator console for the whole Gateway and a device node at once: Limited access drops only operator.admin and keeps Gateway-wide write, read and approvals scopes, and since Tony's phone already holds two Control UI entries with admin scope, what is new is the node role and the hosted push relay.

Tony's phone only: operator scopes are not a boundary between people, so on a second adult's phone the other adult's agent memory would be readable, and `gateway.roles`, the one feature that could narrow that, refuses the device and setup-code tokens that pairing issues.

iMessage with attachment intake (F002) and the Control UI already on the phone cover most of this, and voice over iMessage (F003) already gives both parents voice memos in and spoken replies out, so the app adds the share sheet, the offline queue, the native inbox and, for Tony alone, a hands-free loop he can interrupt.

App Store builds receive push through OpenClaw's hosted relay, a service outside the tailnet, and iOS suspends the app in the background, so node commands need the app in front and voice is best-effort.
Audio can leave the house even in the native Talk loop: the docs say Apple Speech recognition on iOS may use network services, and the transcript then goes to OpenAI as text like any typed message.

Talk playback uses the Talk speech provider and not the general tts block, a Limited pairing cannot open the app's Talk settings pages, and `--voice-node` is not an option because typed chat and the Listen action need the write scope; plan on the inline Talk control and expect the iPhone's own system voice.

Realtime option: raw audio goes to OpenAI for the whole call, under 30 days of abuse-monitoring retention unless the organisation has Zero Data Retention, it is billed separately from chat, and `talk.realtime` is one gateway-wide block that replaces the native loop instead of sitting beside it.

There is no speaker identification anywhere in the stack: whoever is near the microphone is the user, and the spoken yes that gates a high-impact action in realtime mode does not identify who said it, so a child must not use Talk.

name: Research agent extra readers: read-only browser behind an action firewall hook, and summarize CLI
description: The research helper can also read public pages that need JavaScript, logged out, and pull the text out of long articles, of videos that have captions and of podcasts that publish a transcript. An in-house hook keeps the browser read-only in code (one profile, no typing, no form filling, no uploads, no page scripts); bot walls and logins stop it.
example: Jordan texts: "What does the rec centre page say about spring swim lessons?" The page shows nothing without JavaScript, so research opens it in the logged-out browser and her own agent relays the dates with the link. Or Tony texts a link to a 40-minute video that has captions and asks for the main points.
how: Two readers, on the research agent only. (1) The `browser` tool on the managed `openclaw` profile, with `headless: true` on that profile and `browser.evaluateEnabled: false`. Up to four switches come first: `browser.enabled` (off since M0, and possibly not needed, see below), the browser tool on research's sandbox tool allow list (it is on the sandbox default deny list), the per-agent tool allow, and a place for the browser to live. First choice is the roadmap's sandbox browser container with the LAN blocked, which has a switch of its own (`sandbox.browser.enabled`, off by default and off in today's config, to be turned on for research only); its image has to be built from a source checkout because the npm install does not include the Dockerfile. The sandbox reference says this container browser does not require the top-level `browser.enabled`, while the browser setup page says the agent tool needs it, so try it with `browser.enabled` left off first: if that works, the host's browser control service is never switched on. The fallback is the host's managed profile through `sandbox.browser.allowHostControl` and an explicit host target, which the docs say to keep off for sandboxed agents unless you trust them. (2) A host stdio MCP that wraps `summarize --extract --json` and returns extracted text from articles, and from YouTube videos and podcasts that publish captions or a transcript, without calling a model; the wrapper pins `--firecrawl off`, holds no third-party keys, sets up no transcription fallback and checks the address itself. The firewall (formerly WEB-03): an in-house plugin with `api.on("before_tool_call", handler, { matcher: ["browser"] })`, default-deny and failing closed. It rejects any `profile`, `target` or `node` other than the one assigned to the agent (a missing profile is filled in or blocked, because an omitted profile means the default one) and rejects `systemProfile`, `into`, `domains` and `dashboard`. Of the tool's 24 actions it allows only a listed read-only subset (for example status, tabs, open, navigate, focus, close, snapshot, text, screenshot). `act` and `upload` are not on that list in this build, which blocks every act kind at once: `batch`, `evaluate`, `press`, `clickCoords`, `drag`, `wait`, `resize`, `type`, `fill`, `select` and `click`. If a page later proves unreadable without scrolling, `act` comes back only for kinds on an allowlist of its own (`scrollIntoView`, `hover`), each with an eval case. The hook reads the URL from `targetUrl` first and `url` second, looks inside a nested `request` object, and blocks any call whose top-level and nested kinds differ. Unknown agent, missing field, unknown action or kind, or a parse error returns a block; the runner itself blocks the call if the handler throws or times out. Research reads the open web, so there is no site allowlist here; navigation stays http and https under the private-network block in F019 (formerly WEB-01). Not built here: the exact-hostname allowlist and the ask-a-parent-before-typing approval branch, whose only consumer is the roadmap's M6 jobs agent.
caveats: Bot walls, logins, CAPTCHAs and two-factor prompts stop it. The bundled browser skill tells the agent to report them as manual steps, and the docs say sandboxed browser sessions are more likely to be flagged as bots.

The sandbox browser image cannot be built from the npm install; it needs a source checkout. The host alternative needs allowHostControl, which the docs say to keep off for sandboxed agents unless you trust them.

The hook sees tool parameters, not page meaning: a click carries a snapshot ref, not the button's label, so code cannot tell 'Next' from 'Submit'. That is why clicks are blocked outright in this read-only build.
A navigation check in a hook sees the URL the agent asked for, not where redirects or page scripts go next; the private-network block in F019 is the backstop.
With open and navigate allowed, a link straight to a file is saved into the managed downloads directory without the download action ever being called.

The parameter names come from the installed 2026.9.7 browser tool schema and can change with any update. Default-deny keeps a new action blocked until someone allows it, but the hook needs a contract test after every OpenClaw update.

summarize runs on the host, outside the SSRF policy that covers web_fetch and the browser, and has its own third-party extraction fallbacks; the wrapper must switch those off and check the address itself.
An independent evaluation on live websites found web agents much less competent than earlier benchmarks suggested, so expect misses on complex pages.

The extractor uses published captions and podcast transcripts first; its README says transcription is a fallback that has to be configured. The wrapper holds no keys and sets none up, so expect nothing back for a video without captions or a podcast without a published transcript; local transcription would be a later add-on.
corrections: The catalog says to 'use the host profile'; because research must stay sandboxed, the browser tool defaults to the sandbox browser, and the host profile needs `agents.defaults.sandbox.browser.allowHostControl: true` plus an explicit host target.

The catalog's install line names the tap formula steipete/tap/summarize (as the bundled skill does); the upstream README opened in this run gives `npm install --global @steipete/summarize` or `brew install summarize`.
unverified: `--youtube auto` and the optional Apify token appear in the bundled skill but not on the upstream README; check `summarize --help` after install.
How often rec-portal and store pages block a headless, logged-out browser was not measured.
The hook contract was read, but the browser parameter names come from the tool's schema source and were not observed in a live hook event.
Whether `ctx.agentId` carries the sub-agent's id when research runs as a spawned session; every per-agent rule depends on it.
Whether the hook sees the browser call before the tool applies its own defaults (profile, target), so that 'must be present' can be enforced.
Whether script-rendered pages can be read with the `act` action off (no `wait`, `click` or scrolling); any kind allowed back needs its own eval case.
What summarize returns for a video without captions when no transcription engine is configured (an error or an empty result); the README does not say and the tool is not installed.

Whether the sandbox browser gives research a working `browser` tool with the top-level `browser.enabled` left false: the sandbox configuration page says it is not required, the browser setup page says the tool needs it.
safety: The research agent holds no private data, no memory and no accounts, and this browser is a managed profile with none of the family's signed-in sessions, so an injected page has nothing to steal. What a real browser adds is a way to act, so the limits on profile, target and actions live in code and fail closed, page script evaluation is off in config, and the home network is out of reach (the egress guardrails in F019). The hook is in-house code on the security boundary: one parsing mistake is a bypass, so it gets its own injection eval cases before the browser is switched on. No profile on this browser ever holds a login, and CAPTCHAs are reported, never solved.

name: House devices by text: Hue and Sonos through a stateless home agent, with a read-only goodnight check (later option: Home Assistant as the single route, with Sonos announcements)
description: A parent texts Happy to switch Hue rooms and scenes by name, or to play a Sonos favourite, pause everything or set a room's volume, inside a room allowlist, a hard volume cap and quiet hours enforced in code. Separately, at 22:30 a parent gets a text only if lights or speakers are still on; that check switches nothing. The first build uses two command-line tools on the Mac mini. A later option replaces them and is not an addition: Home Assistant, running in a VM on the Mac mini and reached through its own MCP Server integration, puts Hue, Sonos and the LG TV on one list of devices a parent has exposed, and adds the one thing the command-line tools have no command for: a parent texts 'announce: ...' and the Sonos speakers say it over the music, which is turned down and then restored. OpenClaw 2026.9.7 has no Home Assistant, HomeKit, Matter or MQTT integration of its own, so that route goes through Home Assistant's MCP server. It is worth an always-on VM mainly if the announcements are wanted or the VM already exists for the kids' kitchen speaker (a later step of the kids agent, F072).
example: Jordan texts: 'Downstairs lights off and pause the music.' At 22:30, only if something is on: 'Still on: family room lights, living room Sonos.' With the later Home Assistant option: 'announce: the bus leaves in ten minutes', and the living room and family room speakers say it.
how: Step 1, read-only (F081): a command payload with no model runs openhue and sonos status on the Gateway host at 22:30 and prints `NO_REPLY` when everything is off; nothing is actuated. Step 2, switching: a sandboxed, stateless home agent reached by `sessions_spawn` holds two in-house plugins. Hue (F076) wraps the openhue CLI on the host, with the bridge key in ~/.openhue/config.yaml, a room allowlist and quiet hours in code. Sonos (F077) wraps the sonos CLI: favourites and allowlisted scenes only, a volume cap and a lower night cap in code; it needs the macOS Local Network permission for the gateway's node process, or `--ip` per speaker. Scheduled bedtime scenes are left to the Hue app, and the other bundled device skills stay uninstalled. Later option, Home Assistant as the single route (a separate, large piece of work that replaces the two plugins; the home agent stays): run Home Assistant OS in a VM on the Mac mini (the roadmap already plans this VM for the kids' kitchen speaker, a later step of the kids agent, F072). Add the Hue, Sonos and LG webOS integrations, then the 'Model Context Protocol Server' integration; turn off 'Expose all LLM APIs' and expose only the wanted entities. In OpenClaw add mcp.servers.<name> with url http://<ha-host>:8123/api/mcp, transport 'streamable-http' written out (when it is omitted OpenClaw uses sse), and the Home Assistant long-lived token in headers.Authorization, supplied through a secret reference and not a config literal (auth 'oauth' with openclaw mcp login is the documented alternative). This Gateway uses tools.profile 'minimal', which hides MCP tools, so grant them only to the stateless home agent by listing the <server>__<tool> names in that agent's alsoAllow and in its sandbox tool allow list (tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow); no other agent then sees the server. Write toolFilter.include after a live probe (openclaw mcp doctor <name> --probe), since it selects tools by name. The registry before_tool_call hook stays as the second, fail-closed gate and enforces quiet hours. Announcements: Home Assistant's Sonos integration plays speech with its `announce` option as an overlay, lowering the music and restoring the volume afterwards; it needs TCP port 1443 on each speaker to be reachable from the Home Assistant host. Because the MCP server offers intents and exposed scripts only, a parent writes one Home Assistant script that wraps the announce call and exposes it, and picks a local speech engine in Home Assistant, since its text-to-speech page also lists cloud engines. The trigger is deterministic: a `before_dispatch` claim on a fixed prefix such as `announce:` from an adult's handle, so no agent that reads web results decides to speak to the house. The code that claims the text then starts the Home Assistant script itself, with no model turn, through Home Assistant's REST API (`/api/services/<domain>/<service>` with the same host-side bearer token); that call path is a design choice and was not tried. The first version offers a short list of fixed phrases; the parent's own words, verbatim, come later, and model-written text never. Text length, volume, quiet hours (G001), a speaker allowlist and a daily cap are enforced in code.
caveats: This switches things in the house, so the room allowlist, the volume caps and quiet hours are enforced in plugin code and not by the prompt.
Neither command-line tool is installed, and the bridge and the two speakers (living room and family room) come from the 9 Oct scan and were not re-checked.

Play-by-search is left out of this build: it would use the music service already linked in the Sonos app, so Happy would hold no music login, but auto-playing the first search hit has no content filter. Favourites and saved scenes only.
The Hue app can already switch lights at a set time and when you leave home, so Happy's part at night is the reminder and not the switching.

Home Assistant is a replacement route to the same devices, not an addition: running both doubles the paths to the same lamp. With only Hue, two Sonos speakers and one TV in the house, it pays off mainly if the announcements or the kids' kitchen speaker (F072) are also wanted.

Home Assistant option: the VM is one more service to patch, back up and bring back after every reboot and FileVault unlock, and until it is up every home tool fails. Home Assistant's macOS page documents VirtualBox (UTM only as a fallback for people used to virtual machines) and points anyone not familiar with virtual machines to a dedicated board.

Home Assistant option: its MCP server offers Assist intents plus any scripts exposed to Assist, not arbitrary actions, and supports neither notifications nor sampling, so Happy can only ask and Home Assistant cannot push a state change. Because the tools are generic intents, toolFilter.include narrows verbs, not device classes; the exposure list in Home Assistant and a before_tool_call check on each call's target are the real limits.

Home Assistant option: 'Expose all LLM APIs' and 'Require an administrator account' are both on by default, and new entities in the cover domain (garage doors and gates) are exposed to Assist by default. Tighten the first before OpenClaw connects and review the exposure list after each device is added.

Home Assistant option: the long-lived token is a ten-year credential for Home Assistant's APIs as one user; the exposed-entity limit applies to the MCP tools, not to the token, so it stays host-side and is rotated by hand.
Home Assistant option: state text it returns (now-playing titles, device names) is third-party text read by an agent that can actuate; allowlists and caps in code have to bound the result.

Home Assistant option: a HomeKit accessory can pair with only one controller, so the LG TV stays in Apple Home and joins Home Assistant through the webOS integration. That brings 'TV off by text' (the integration's page lists turning the TV off; turning it on needs an extra automation); a fixed nightly cut-off stays with the TV's own Power Off Timer.

Announcements reach only the two Sonos speakers (living room and family room in the 9 Oct scan), and Home Assistant's Sonos page warns that older Sonos hardware or S1 firmware may not fully support them. A talking house at the wrong moment is worse than no feature: quiet hours and a low daily cap matter more than voice quality.

Without Home Assistant there is no good announcement route: Sonos documents its audio-clip command under the cloud Control API, which would put a Sonos account token on the gateway, and the sonos command-line tool has no announce command (its play-uri sets the speaker to the new audio and documents no way to bring the music back).

The goodnight text is an unprompted, non-urgent text late in the evening. The notification policy (G001) drops such a text outside its allowed hours and does not send it later, so either the allowed hours reach 22:30 or the check runs earlier; otherwise the check runs every night and nobody hears from it.

name: Printed pages from Happy: the Sunday fridge sheet and other pages it makes, plus 'print this' when away from home
description: Happy sends pages to the home printer: the ones it makes itself (the Sunday fridge sheet, the emergency card) and, when a parent texts 'print this', a PDF or photo they attach or a link that points straight at a PDF or an image, with a copies cap. Ordinary web pages are not printed. A phone on the home Wi-Fi can already print by itself, so the on-request part earns its keep mainly when the parent is away from home.
example: On Sunday the week sheet prints by itself: the week's events and chore turns, first names and times only. Or Tony, still at work, texts a permission-slip PDF with 'print this, one copy', so it is on the printer when he gets home.
how: Two parts over one print queue, which is added once on the Mac mini with lpadmin. (1) Pages Happy makes: a scheduled command job with no model call runs a reviewed script that renders the Sunday fridge sheet (the week's schedule and chore turns) from the household store (F031) and the family calendar (F009) and sends it with `lp -d <queue> -n 1`, with no chat message; the emergency card (CRT-13) goes to the same queue when a parent asks. Where the chore turns come from has to be built with this entry: the household store's first version has only its schedule and fact tools and no chore rota, so either a parent sets the rota by text as a fact in that store and the script steps through it week by week, or this entry adds a rota table and tool of its own; until one of the two exists the sheet prints the calendar week only. (2) 'Print this': an in-house plugin calls `lp -d <queue> -n <copies>` on the host with a copies cap in code. It downloads an https link itself, because web_fetch returns text and not the file, and prints the download only when it is a PDF or an image, both of which the print system takes directly; a link to an ordinary web page is refused. A texted file needs attachment intake first (`channels.imessage.includeAttachments`, F002).
caveats: Canon's spec sheet for the PIXMA PRO-100 lists AirPrint, so an iPhone on the same home network can already print a PDF or photo to it by itself. Happy's gain is printing pages it produces (the week sheet, formerly HOM-14 and now part of this entry, and the emergency card in CRT-13) and printing when nobody is on that Wi-Fi.
The one-time print queue on the Mac mini has not been added, and a driverless queue for this printer has not been tried.
The fridge sheet cannot run before the household store (F031) and the calendar read (F009) exist.

'Print this' handles files, not web pages: the printing system's own guide lists text, PostScript, PDF and image files as what it reads directly, so a link has to point straight at a PDF or an image. Printing or saving a web page stays a two-tap job on the phone.
unverified: Whether a driverless (IPP Everywhere) queue created with lpadmin works with this printer; Canon lists AirPrint, but the queue was not created.
The checks against private-network addresses in the download step are a design requirement, not an existing plugin feature.
'No destination configured' comes from the 9 Oct check and was not re-run.

How the no-model fridge-sheet script reads its data was not tried: F009 gives agents a read-only calendar tool and F031 an agent tool over a SQLite file, so the script needs its own read of both (the same read-only gog account from the command line, and the store's file) outside any agent turn.

How the chore rota is entered and stored was never specified. The chore-rota entry removed in round 1 (F039) left only a note to keep the rota as rows in the household store, and the store's first version (F031) has schedule and fact tools only; the single-fact route was not tried.
safety: Printing goes to one named queue with a copies cap enforced in code. The fridge sheet is made by a script with no model in the path and shows first names and times only, because guests read the fridge. 'Print this' acts only on a parent's own request. A link to print is fetched from the host at an address the agent passes in, which is a way out for an agent that holds memory and reads search results; the plugin should accept only an https link that appears word for word in the parent's own message, must refuse private-network addresses, and should print the download only if it is a PDF or an image. These checks are design requirements to build and test, not existing features.

name: Multi-day family project with check-ins
description: A parent hands Happy a project with an end date (birthday party, weekend trip, garage clean-out). Happy keeps one project note with decisions and open items, texts a check-in every few days listing what is still open (it picks the gap itself, inside limits set when the project starts), and stops when the date passes. Research happens only when the parent asks for it in chat: a check-in can remind and list, not browse. The one-shot plan in F028 keeps no state and sends no check-ins.
example: Plan our 10-year-old's birthday party for Saturday the 14th: 10 kids, indoor, under 300 dollars. Check in with me every few days until it is sorted.
how:
Held by the asking parent's

-main. State: one project note (memory/projects/.md through the F041 write path, or home-store rows from F031) with goal, end date, decisions, open items and a review date. The note records only what the parent typed or confirmed, written in a turn that carried no web or research results. Check-ins: one isolated automation per project, created through the `automations` tool on

-main with a `pacing` object (`min`, `max`; `--pacing-min` and `--pacing-max` are the CLI spelling), so each run can call `automations(action: "next_check")` and be clamped to those bounds. The job's tool cap holds the note or home-store read tools plus `automations` (inside an automation run that tool is limited to the run's own job) and never `sessions_spawn` or a web tool; announce to the owner; NO_REPLY when nothing is due; the run removes its own job after the end date. Hard prerequisites before `automations` is allowed on

-main: the fail-closed before_tool_call pin must also match `automations`/`cron` add and update and refuse webhook delivery, completion and failure destinations, and any recipient other than the asking parent; and `cron.triggers.enabled: false`, so the tool does not offer script payloads, trigger scripts or stream commands. The grant itself has a second gate: every Happy agent runs sandboxed and `automations` is on the sandbox default deny list (beside `browser` and `computer`), so it must also be named in

-main's sandbox tool allow list (`tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow`), or a sandboxed turn never gets the tool; the reminders entry (F007) needs the same line. Research legs: `sessions_spawn` to the stateless `research` agent with `runTimeoutSeconds` and `completionTarget: "parent"`, in interactive turns only, so

-main reviews the result privately before it texts anything. Decisions are plain proposals in chat. `/goal` is not the durable state here: the 04:00 reset wipes it.
depends_on: F041 memory write path or F031 home-store

F007 automations tool on

-main, allowed twice: in the per-agent tool allow and in the sandbox tool allow list (`tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow`), because `automations` is on the sandbox default deny list
F019 research agent
G009 delivery pin, extended to cover automations/cron add and update and to refuse webhook delivery
G001 notification policy
decision: Jordan as a command owner
cron.triggers.enabled: false (set in G003, which absorbed AUT-08)

decision: how a check-in job gets past the F007 hook rule that a reminder job created by a parent's agent carries an empty tool list (one more exact tool list admitted by the hook, or the open items carried in the job message)
caveats: Scheduled runs do not get MEMORY.md injected, so a check-in must read the project note with a tool or carry the state in the job message.
A job created from chat is capped to the tools the creating turn had and cannot be widened later, so a check-in can never do more than the parent's own main agent.
The conversation resets every morning at 04:00 and that also wipes any /goal; the project note is the only continuity between days.
Every check-in is a cloud model turn. Pace in days, not minutes, and cap active projects per person (three is plenty).
No bookings, purchases or invitations sent: the output is options, links and drafts. A static checklist is still easier in a shared Notes or Reminders list; Happy adds the nudging and the research.

Command-owner status is gateway-wide: an owner can ask their agent to list, inspect, update, run or remove any job on the gateway, whoever created it. Once Jordan is an owner, each parent's agent can read and change the other's check-in jobs, so job messages must not carry private detail.

The F041 plan refuses memory writes in a turn tainted by web results, and a turn that received a research result is tainted. Research findings therefore cannot be saved into the project note in that turn: they stay in the chat thread, and the note holds only what the parent states or confirms afterwards.

OpenClaw's own guidance is to deny the scheduling tool by default on any agent that handles untrusted content (docs/gateway/security/tool-permissions.md).

-main reads search snippets, so granting it `automations` is a deliberate exception that rests on the delivery pin and on triggers staying off.

The reminders entry (F007) has the delivery-pin hook require an empty tool list on a reminder job, so that a timed run can only produce text, and to that hook a check-in is the same call: a parent's agent adding a job. A check-in that reads the project note and sets its own next gap needs tools, so one of two things has to be decided first: the hook admits one more exact tool list (the note-read tool and `automations`, nothing else), or the check-in carries the open items in its job message and keeps the empty list. Whether self-pacing and self-removal still work with the empty list is already on the open-checks list.
safety:
-main holds the note and never browses; `research` does every web leg, has no memory, and as a sub-agent can never get the message, cron or gateway tools. The `automations` tool is itself a send path: a job can name any chat as its delivery target or post its result to a webhook URL.

-main holds memory and reads search snippets, so the recipient pin must cover `automations`/`cron` calls, not only `message`, and must refuse webhook mode before the tool is granted. Check-in runs carry no web tool and no `sessions_spawn`; that is the hard limit. The rule that handoff text carries dates, ages and budget only (never names, school or address) is prompt text, not enforcement. With the pin in place nothing on the never list is reachable: there is no payment, booking or outbound-to-strangers tool anywhere in the chain.
unverified: Whether a custom-session job (`--session session:<id>`) is exempt from the daily reset policy, which would let check-ins keep conversational context.
Whether memory read tools can be named in a job tool cap for a sandboxed agent on 2026.9.7; test at build time.
That research handoffs return results with agent-to-agent off and session visibility self (already an open item in the roadmap).
Whether the gateway accepts webhook delivery or an arbitrary recipient on a job that an agent creates from an iMessage owner turn. The tool description offers both; it was not tested.
Whether next_check and self-removal stay callable when the job's tool cap leaves out `automations`.
Whether the F041 path hook, written for memory/*.md, admits a memory/projects/ subfolder.

That an isolated check-in run of a sandboxed agent is filtered by the same sandbox tool list as a chat turn, so that one `tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow` entry for `automations` covers both. The installed source drops a built-in sandbox deny for a tool that the allow list names; this was read, not run.
